host.note: Rented c7g.xlarge, aarch64. Counter is cntvct_el0 (fixed rate, coarser than the core clock); PMCCNTR_EL0 is gated, so a dependency-chain average over the virtual counter resolves the leak.

regenerable: on an aarch64 Neoverse-V1 host: taskset -c 2 python3 pairs/kyberslash/graviton/measure_arm.py

codegen.note: gcc emits a hardware udiv at -Os only (O0=0, Os=1, O2=0), the same size-only pattern as x86; here the compiler narrows the signed-int source to an UNSIGNED udiv where the x86 build emits a signed idiv. Confirmed by the committed disassembly.

udiv_latency_operand_dependent.note: Serial dependency chain. Unlike the x86 divider, which resolves no operand-dependent step in the same serial chain, the Neoverse-V1 udiv latency RISES with dividend magnitude (more significant quotient bits cost more): this is the leak.

operand_magnitude_leak.note: The exploitable signal is operand-magnitude: low coefficients (dividend < 3329, quotient 0) run faster than high coefficients (quotient >= 1). This is NOT a single-coefficient boundary step.

single_bit_boundary_step.note: Adjacent coefficients 832 (dividend 3328, quotient 0) and 833 (dividend 3330, quotient 1) are indistinguishable in udiv time: the single-bit recovery step is SUB-NOISE on this hardware divider, unlike the software division the published Cortex-A7 attack used.

end_to_end_coeff_to_bit_Os.note: Two-class over the real coeff_to_bit, min-of-9 batches, 10 repeats. Low class = coeff in [0,832] (quotient 0), high = [1664,3328] (quotient >= 1). The operand-magnitude delta a full reduction call carries.

dudect_on_aarch64.note: CORRECTED 2026-08-25, and the correction changes the reason rather than the verdict. An earlier revision reported this control as clean because its budget-invariant tau 'converged downward with measurement count, the signature of a null effect'. That inference was invalid: E[tau^2] ~ d^2/4 + 1/n falls with n for EVERY effect size, so a downward tau proves nothing, and only the asymptote separates a null (slope -1/2 on log-log) from a fixed effect (slope 0). Worse, the statistic it was computed from is not meaningful on this counter.
dudect_on_aarch64.counter_resolution_finding: cntvct_el0 quantises the measurement far too coarsely for a per-call test of this function: a coeff_to_bit call is 7 or 8 ticks. Over the 400000 measurements of that run (summarised here; the raw dump is not committed and regenerates only on an aarch64 host) there are only 99 distinct tick values and 86% of them are exactly 7. dudect's crop ladder therefore contains crops holding a single repeated value, on which Welch's t is 0/0; the earlier |t| trajectory was dominated by that artifact, not by a timing difference.

verdict_permutation.statistic: max |Welch t| over dudect's first-order crop ladder, crops with zero within-class variance excluded
verdict_permutation.tool: bin/dudect_permute.py, 2000 label shuffles stratified within batch

dudect_on_aarch64.verdict: not detected: the per-call statistical test does not resolve the division on this host. This is a RESOLUTION limit, not evidence of absence. The serial-chain measurement resolves the operand-magnitude effect at 0.41 ticks per udiv, which is below one tick of this counter, so no per-call test on cntvct_el0 can see it at any budget. The cycle-accurate PMU is privileged on a virtualised instance, which is why the coarse counter is the one available.
dudect_on_aarch64.reproduce: patch dudect.h cpucycles to read cntvct_el0 and _mm_mfence to __sync_synchronize, drop the x86 headers, gcc -Os dudect_coeff_driver.c + pairs/kyberslash/src/vulnerable.c -lm, DUDECT_RAW_DUMP set, taskset -c 2; then bin/dudect_permute.py on the dump.
dudect_on_aarch64._counter_resolution_note: Corrected 2026-09-02: the finding used to say 'Over 400000 committed measurements'; the dump behind the per-call verdict was never committed, and the paper now says so.

recovery_assessment.note: Attempted per the tier-A goal; not feasible cheaply on Graviton3. The one-bit-per-coefficient recovery needs the adjacent-coefficient (single-bit boundary) step, which is sub-noise here; the resolvable signal is operand magnitude (batch estimator only), and a per-call timing test reads clean on the virtual counter. The published recovery used the Cortex-A7 software-division routine (tens of cycles, sharply operand-dependent), a different and louder mechanism. KyberSlash therefore stays tier C, now with a measured reason rather than an assumed one.
